{{Short description|Concept in mathematical logic}}{{More citations needed|date=November 2025}}{{no footnotes|date=January 2025}}
In [[mathematical logic]], a [[theory (mathematical logic)|theory]] of a [[formal language|language]] is '''complete''' if it is [[consistent theory|consistent]] and it [[Turnstile (symbol)|proves]] every [[Well-formed formula#Closed formulas|closed formula]] with which it is not inconsistent. That is to say, a consistent theory <math>T</math> is complete if, for every [[Sentence (mathematical logic)|sentence]] <math>\varphi</math> in the language, either <math>T \vdash \varphi</math> holds or <math>T \cup \{\varphi\}</math> is inconsistent. Another common definition, that is equivalent if the [[formal system]] satisfies the [[principle of explosion]], requires instead that either <math>\varphi</math> or its negation <math>\neg \varphi</math> is provable from <math>T</math>. Using this definition, consistency of <math>T</math> follows automatically if "either" and "or" are read as exclusive disjunction, and it thus can be omitted from the definition. If <math>T</math> is furthermore [[deductively closed]], completeness reduces to the concise condition that exactly one of <math>\varphi</math> and <math>\neg \varphi</math> is contained in <math>T</math> for every sentence <math>\varphi</math>. Recursively axiomatizable [[List of first-order theories|first-order theories]] that are consistent and rich enough to allow general mathematical reasoning to be formulated cannot be complete, as demonstrated by [[Gödel's first incompleteness theorem]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251230121332/https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Completeness_(in_logic) |title=Completeness (in logic) - Encyclopedia of Mathematics |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Mathematics |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Completeness_(in_logic) |archive-date=30 December 2025 |access-date=6 July 2026}}</ref>

This syntactic sense of ''complete'' is distinct from the semantic notion of a [[Completeness (logic)#Semantic completeness|complete formal system]], which asserts that for every theory that can be formulated in the formal system, all semantically valid statements are provable theorems (for an appropriate sense of "semantically valid"). [[Gödel's completeness theorem]] is about this latter kind of completeness.

== Complete theories ==
Complete theories are closed under a number of conditions internally modelling the [[T-schema]]:
* For a set of formulas <math>S</math>: <math>A \land B \in S</math> if and only if <math>A \in S</math> and <math>B \in S</math>,
* For a set of formulas <math>S</math>: <math>A \lor B \in S</math> if and only if <math>A \in S</math> or <math>B \in S</math>.

Maximal consistent sets are a fundamental tool in the [[model theory]] of [[classical logic]] and [[modal logic]]. Their existence in a given case is usually a straightforward consequence of [[Zorn's lemma]], based on the idea that a [[contradiction]] involves use of only finitely many premises. In the case of modal logics, the collection of maximal consistent sets extending a theory ''T'' (closed under the necessitation rule) can be given the structure of a [[Kripke semantics|model]] of ''T'', called the canonical model.

==Examples==

Some examples of complete theories are:
* [[Presburger arithmetic]]
* [[Tarski's axioms]] for [[Euclidean geometry]]
* The theory of [[Dense order|dense]] [[linear order]]s without endpoints
* The theory of [[algebraically closed field]]s of a given [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]]
* The theory of [[real closed field]]s
* Every [[Morley's categoricity theorem|uncountably categorical]] [[Countable set|countable]] theory
* Every [[omega-categorical theory|countably categorical]] countable theory
* A [https://math.stackexchange.com/q/159124 group of three elements]
* [[True arithmetic]] or any other [[elementary diagram]] or complete theory of a [[structure (mathematical logic)|structure]] (see {{section link|Theory (mathematical logic)|Theories associated with a structure}})
